web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Business Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: How the Business Got Here — From Blue Ribbon Sports to the 'Win Now' Reset
question: How did NIKE, Inc. evolve from a scrappy Japanese-shoe importer into a $46.4 billion global athletic titan, and why have its three major strategic cycles always hinged on the tension between performance innovation and distribution reach?

epigraph.quote: We are in the middle innings of our comeback, and it starts with putting sport and the athlete back at the center of everything we do.
epigraph.author: Elliott Hill, President & CEO, NIKE, Inc. (FY2026)

web_blocks.title: 1.1 From Track-Side Trunk Sales to the Swoosh Ecosystem (1964–1990)

web_blocks.html: NIKE, Inc. began in January 1964 as Blue Ribbon Sports (BRS). University of Oregon track coach Bill Bowerman and former runner Phil Knight each contributed $500 to start the firm [1]. Knight's Stanford MBA thesis argued that Japanese running shoes could undercut German rivals Adidas and Puma on price without sacrificing quality. BRS first served as the U.S. distributor for Onitsuka Tiger, selling shoes from Knight's Plymouth Valiant trunk at Northwest track meets. When Onitsuka moved to end the contract in 1971, Knight and Bowerman broke away. They paid design student Carolyn Davidson $35 for the Swoosh logo and launched their own NIKE footwear line. That pivot led to Bowerman's waffle-iron outsole patent and an IPO on December 2, 1980 [1].

What set Nike apart from regional footwear brands in the 1970s and 1980s was not factory ownership. Knight avoided owning plants from day one, contracting production to low-cost Asian partners instead. Instead, Nike paired visible cushioning tech with memorable athlete storytelling. The 1979 debut of Air cushioning in the Tailwind and the 1984 signing of NBA rookie Michael Jordan changed basketball shoes forever [1]. Footwear shifted from basic gym gear into global cultural currency. By 1990, Nike had passed Reebok to lead the U.S. athletic footwear market. That success built a clear flywheel: elite athletes proved performance credibility, credibility fueled mass lifestyle demand, and lifestyle scale funded bigger R&D and marketing budgets.

web_blocks.title: 1.2 Three Distinct Operating Cycles and Strategic Pivots (1990–2024)

web_blocks.html: Over the past 35 years, Nike's operating history has moved through three distinct cycles. Each cycle tested how management balanced product innovation against channel reach and brand scarcity. The first cycle (1990–2005) centered on global category expansion. Nike grew annual revenue from $2 billion to nearly $14 billion by building subsidiaries across Europe and Asia and buying Converse in 2003 [1]. Tighter factory audits and supply-chain controls also helped the company survive late-1990s labor boycotts and Asian financial crisis inventory gluts [1].

The second cycle (2006–2019), led by longtime CEO Mark Parker, marked the golden era of category offense and sneaker culture. Nike reorganized teams around specific sports and launched Flyknit and carbon-plated Vaporfly super-shoes. Management also built the SNKRS app, turning limited Jordan and Dunk drops into high-margin digital lotteries [1, 10]. Greater China became a multi-billion-dollar growth engine with operating margins above 30% [1, 10]. Revenue rose from $15 billion in FY2006 to $39.1 billion in FY2019, while gross margins held steady between 44% and 46% [20].

The third cycle (2020–2024), led by former ServiceNow and eBay chief John Donahoe, broke sharply from Nike's wholesale roots. In June 2020, management launched Consumer Direct Acceleration (CDA). The plan aimed to lift digital sales to 50% of revenue (40% owned digital) by FY2025 while cutting roughly half of Nike's wholesale accounts [13]. Pandemic stimulus initially hid the structural risks of that shift. Revenue jumped from $37.4 billion in FY2020 to $51.2 billion in FY2023 and $51.4 billion in FY2024, with gross margin peaking at 46.0% in FY2022 [10, 20]. Beneath those gains, however, Nike lost running shelf space at specialty stores and over-supplied three lifestyle lines—Air Force 1, Dunk, and Air Jordan 1—until buyers grew tired of them.

web_blocks.takeaway: Every major Nike drawdown has followed distribution or franchise over-extension, and every recovery has required restoring product innovation and retail partner alignment.

web_blocks.title: 1.3 The FY2025–FY2026 Reset: 'Win Now', 'Sport Offense', and 'Pace'

web_blocks.html: By mid-2024, the bill for Consumer Direct Acceleration had come due. FY2025 revenue fell 10% to $46,309 million, and net income plunged 44% from $5,700 million to $3,219 million [1, 4, 9]. Excess Classics inventory forced heavy markdowns and off-price liquidations [1, 4, 9]. In October 2024, the Board recalled 32-year Nike veteran Elliott Hill from retirement as President and CEO [6]. Former Pfizer and CVS Health finance chief Dave Denton joined as EVP and CFO in August 2026 [8]. Hill immediately launched the 'Win Now' tactical reset. He cut supply of oversaturated Air Force 1, Dunk, and Air Jordan 1 styles, rebuilt ties with wholesale partners like Foot Locker and Dick's Sporting Goods, and reinvested in performance running [6].

In FY2026 (ended May 31, 2026), those steps stabilized top-line revenue at $46,398 million, flat reported and down 2% currency-neutral [1, 2]. Gross margin rose 20 bps to 42.9%, though net income still slipped 3% to $3,108 million [1, 2]. In October 2026, Q1 FY2027 revenue fell 4% to $11.2 billion on a 22% drop in Greater China and a 28% slide at Converse [3, 22]. Alongside those results, Hill and Denton unveiled 'Pace,' a multi-year transformation built atop the 'Sport Offense' reorganization [3, 7]. Then at NIKE's November 17, 2026 Investor Day (Form 8-K, Ex. 99.1), management introduced the 'Full Stride Ahead' strategy—anchored on three pillars (EPIC, CONNECTED, FAST) and focused on five priority Performance Sports plus Sportswear across 23 priority countries—while confirming a steeper near-term earnings trough. Management reaffirmed FY2027 guidance for a high-single-digit revenue decline, ~6% adjusted operating margin, and $1.15 to $1.35 adjusted EPS (excluding ~$0.15/share of Pace severance), while targeting ~$1.3 billion in cumulative Pace pre-tax restructuring charges ($0.3B in FY2026, $0.3B in FY2027), a return to market-level revenue growth only in FY2029, ~$2.5 billion in annualized Pace run-rate savings by FY2031, and 12–14% operating margins ($3.00–$3.50 adjusted EPS) by FY2031.

web_blocks.title: The Core Lesson of Nike's History
paragraphs: Nike's asset-light manufacturing model delivers strong capital efficiency when product heat is high, because factories sit on partner balance sheets. When product heat cools, however, fixed demand-creation spending ($4.75 billion in FY2026) and store leases drive sharp operating deleverage. That dynamic cut operating income nearly in half from $6,311 million in FY2024 to $3,797 million in FY2026 [1, 20].

web_blocks.mechanism: After two decades of rapid expansion to ~$5.0B revenue by 2017, Under Armour suffered from North American wholesale over-distribution, Sports Authority's bankruptcy, and an inability to build credible lifestyle or technical running franchises. A brief post-pandemic bounce to $5.9B in FY2023 gave way to renewed markdowns and deliberate wholesale pruning.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Revenue stagnated back around $5.0B by FY2026—effectively zero net top-line growth over nine years—forcing founder Kevin Plank to return as CEO to execute a multi-year brand reset [18].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: In athletic apparel and footwear, channel misalignment and lifestyle/innovation gaps do not self-correct in one or two quarters; regaining full-price shelf velocity takes multi-year product cycles and disciplined supply control.

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand why NIKE, Inc. is fighting through one of the most consequential resets in modern consumer-brand history, you and I have to start in the trunk of a Plymouth Valiant in 1964. Phil Knight, fresh out of Stanford Business School, and Bill Bowerman, the legendary Oregon track coach, put $500 each into Blue Ribbon Sports on a simple insight: Japanese factories could make better running shoes for less money than German giants Adidas and Puma. Knight never wanted to own a single factory. Instead, he wanted to own the athlete's mind, the patented sole geometry, and the distribution relationship at the finish line.

For fifty-five years, that formula printed money. Think about the flywheel Knight and longtime CEO Mark Parker perfected. You sign a generational athlete like Michael Jordan or Eliud Kipchoge, you put an unmistakable innovation on their feet—visible Air, Flyknit, or a carbon-plated Vaporfly—and you let the track or the hardwood validate the product. Once the purists buy it, the streetwear crowd adopts it, and you can sell millions of pairs of Air Force 1s or Dunks at rich margins without reinventing the mold. Between 2006 and 2019, Nike scaled from $15 billion to $39.1 billion in revenue while keeping gross margins locked in a remarkably tight 44% to 46% band.

So what broke? Between 2020 and 2024, you watched a textbook case of how a brilliant short-term thesis can quietly cannibalize a moat. Under former tech executive John Donahoe, Nike rolled out Consumer Direct Acceleration in June 2020, declaring that digital sales would reach 50% of the business by FY2025. To force shoppers onto Nike.com and the SNKRS app, management walked away from roughly half of its wholesale retail accounts. During the pandemic stimulus boom, the numbers looked magical: revenue topped $51 billion in FY2023 and FY2024, and gross margin briefly hit 46.0% in FY2022.

Yet walk into a specialty running store or a suburban mall in 2023, and you could see the rot. By vacating wholesale shelves, Nike handed prime real estate to hungry challengers like On Holding and Deckers' HOKA, while Adidas staged a fierce comeback under Bjørn Gulden. Worse, Nike leaned too hard on three aging lifestyle cash cows—Air Force 1, Dunk, and Air Jordan 1—flooding the market until sneakerheads stopped lining up. When demand cooled, revenue fell 10% in FY2025 to $46.3 billion, and net income collapsed 44% to $3.22 billion.

That brings us to the present reset under Elliott Hill, a 32-year Nike lifer pulled out of retirement in October 2024, paired with seasoned CFO Dave Denton who joined in August 2026. Hill's 'Win Now' playbook is a deliberate reversal of the Donahoe era: shrink the oversupplied Classics, apologize to wholesale partners like Dick's Sporting Goods and Foot Locker, reorganize teams around specific sports under the 'Sport Offense' model, and launch the 'Pace' program to capture $2.5 billion in annualized run-rate savings by FY2031 at an estimated pre-tax restructuring cost of $1.3 billion. At its November 17, 2026 Investor Day, management formalized the next phase—'Full Stride Ahead,' concentrating resources on five priority Performance Sports plus Sportswear across 23 priority countries—while warning shareholders that the turnaround will take longer to reach the bottom line: FY2027 revenue is guided down high-single digits with adjusted operating margin compressing to roughly 6% ($1.15 to $1.35 adjusted EPS), and market-level revenue growth is not targeted until FY2029.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: History shows Nike rarely loses to a competitor's balance sheet; it loses when management forgets that performance sport credibility is the upstream spring feeding every downstream lifestyle dollar.

book_subsections.title: Inside the Beaverton Playbook: Why Every Nike Cycle Hinges on the Track
paragraphs: Picture yourself standing beside a muddy Pacific Northwest track in 1964, watching Phil Knight pop the trunk of his Plymouth Valiant to hand out Japanese Onitsuka Tiger running shoes to collegiate runners. That scene captures the DNA of NIKE, Inc. better than any corporate slide deck. Knight and Oregon track coach Bill Bowerman put $500 each into Blue Ribbon Sports not to build a manufacturing empire—Knight deliberately avoided owning factories from day one—but to pair superior Asian contract production with relentless on-track credibility. When Onitsuka tried to terminate the partnership in 1971, Knight and Bowerman walked away, paid graphic design student Carolyn Davidson $35 for the Swoosh, patented Bowerman's waffle-iron outsole, and took the company public on December 2, 1980.

Once you see that origin story, the next four decades snap into focus. Every time Nike combined visible biomechanics—like 1979's Air cushioning in the Tailwind or Flyknit and carbon-plated Vaporfly super-shoes—with unmistakable cultural storytelling like the 1984 signing of NBA rookie Michael Jordan, the flywheel spun effortlessly. By 1990, Nike had overtaken Reebok in the U.S. athletic market. Between 1990 and 2005, it scaled from $2 billion to nearly $14 billion, absorbed Converse in 2003, and survived late-1990s labor-practice boycotts and Asian financial crisis inventory gluts by tightening factory auditing. Then, under longtime CEO Mark Parker from 2006 to 2019, Nike turned sneaker scarcity into an art form through the SNKRS app and built Greater China into a multi-billion-dollar engine with operating margins above 30%, growing revenue from $15 billion to $39.1 billion while holding gross margins in a remarkably steady 44% to 46% corridor.

book_subsections.title: The Under Armour Cautionary Tale and the Anatomy of a Reset
paragraphs: Now walk with me into a suburban sporting goods store in 2023 to understand why that 55-year flywheel jammed. Under John Donahoe's June 2020 Consumer Direct Acceleration plan, Nike pledged to push digital revenue to 50% of the business—with 40% owned digital—by FY2025, and walked away from roughly half of its traditional wholesale accounts. Pandemic stimulus initially hid the damage as revenue climbed from $37.4 billion in FY2020 to $51.4 billion in FY2024 and gross margin touched 46.0% in FY2022. On the retail floor, however, vacating specialty running shelves handed prime real estate to On Holding and Deckers' HOKA while Adidas roared back. At the same time, Nike flooded the market with Air Force 1, Dunk, and Air Jordan 1 colorways until collectors stopped caring, triggering a 10% revenue drop to $46,309 million and a 44% net-income collapse to $3,219 million in FY2025.

History offers a sobering warning about how slowly channel mistakes heal. Look at Under Armour: after scaling to roughly $5.0 billion by 2017, wholesale over-distribution, Sports Authority's bankruptcy, and an inability to build credible lifestyle or technical running franchises left Under Armour stuck back around $5.0 billion by FY2026—effectively zero net growth over nine years, forcing founder Kevin Plank back as CEO. That is why Nike's Board recalled 32-year veteran Elliott Hill from retirement in October 2024 and brought in former Pfizer and CVS Health finance chief Dave Denton as CFO in August 2026. Hill's 'Win Now' reset stabilized FY2026 revenue at $46,398 million and nudged gross margin up 20 basis points to 42.9%, though net income still slipped 3% to $3,108 million. With Q1 FY2027 revenue down 4% to $11.2 billion on a 22% Greater China drop and a 28% Converse slump, management followed October's 'Pace' announcement with its November 17, 2026 Investor Day 'Full Stride Ahead' framework—acknowledging FY2027 revenue will fall high-single digits toward an adjusted operating margin trough of roughly 6% ($1.15 to $1.35 adjusted EPS) while absorbing $1.3 billion in Pace restructuring charges before targeting market-level growth in FY2029 and 12–14% operating margins by FY2031.
